title: The Drift Lab
summary: Count electrons through a gate, find the slow drift speed in a copper wire and why a lamp still lights at once.
subject: physics
ncertRef: Section 3.5, Drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
concepts: Speed of the signal versus drift
learningOutcome: The student can find a current from the charge that passes, find the drift speed from I = nAev_d, explain why the signal is fast while the drift is slow, and use mobility.

levels.title: Count the charge
levels.adds: Baseline: current is charge per second, I = Q/t, and the conventional direction is opposite to the electrons (Section 3.2).
hints: The charge that passed is the number of electrons times 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Current is that charge divided by the time in seconds.
Electrons are negative, so the conventional current points the other way.

levels.title: A slow crawl
levels.adds: New idea: I = nAev_d, so the drift speed in a copper wire is only a fraction of a millimetre per second (Ex 3.9, Example 3.1).
hints: Rearrange I = n e A v_d for the drift speed. Convert the area to m².
The time to drift the length is the length divided by the drift speed.
Convert seconds to hours at the end.

levels.title: Thick and thin
levels.adds: New idea: for a fixed current the drift speed is inversely proportional to the area, and the signal travels at the speed of light (Example 3.2).
hints: For a fixed current, v_d is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area.
The electric field that starts every electron drifting travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Signal time is length divided by the speed of light. Give it in nanoseconds.

levels.title: Mobility
levels.adds: More steps: v_d = μE with E = V/L, then I = nAev_d (Section 3.5.1).
hints: The field in the wire is the voltage divided by its length.
Drift speed is the mobility times the field. Take care with the 10⁻³ in μ.
Then the current is n e A v_d, with the area in m² and the speed in m/s.

misconceptions: Electrons race along a wire at nearly the speed of light
A lamp lights at once because electrons travel instantly from the switch
Conventional current flows the same way as the electrons
A thinner wire has a slower drift speed
